h1: Hop freshness across long supply chains
title: Hop Freshness Across Long Supply Chains | Craft Beer School
desc: How hops age on the way to your brewery, what to ask your supplier and how to store pellets so aroma and bitterness hold up.
teaser: Hops lose their best qualities long before they look old. Buying, shipping and storing them cold is most of the job.
standfirst: Alpha acids and aroma oils decline with heat, air and time. If your hops cross oceans and sit in warm sheds, you pay for it in the glass.
sections: A hop cone or pellet holds alpha acids (the source of bitterness), essential oils (the source of aroma) and beta acids. Oxygen, heat and light break these down. Alpha acids oxidise into compounds that are less bitter. The oils lose their fruity, citrus or resinous notes and develop cheesy, stale or onion-like ones. Heat speeds all of it up. Varieties differ widely in how quickly they decline. Aroma-type hops often fade faster than high-alpha bittering types, though this varies. You should ask the supplier for data on the variety you buy.
Ask your supplier the right questions

Ask for the crop year, the alpha acid percentage and, where offered, the hop storage index (HSI), a lab measure of how much a sample has aged. Ask how the hops were packed (pellets in oxygen-barrier foil, vacuum-sealed or flushed with nitrogen) and how they were stored before shipping. Ask whether the supplier ships cold or at ambient temperature and whether a refrigerated container is available for your route.

Treat every hop price as a price for a crop year. A cheap lot from two harvests ago can cost more in lost aroma than it saves on the invoice.

Pellets are more compact and more stable than whole cones. The foil bags should be intact, flat and tight, with little air inside. A bag that has ballooned or lost its vacuum should be tested before use and mentioned to the supplier. Keep the original packs sealed until brew day.

The biggest risk is time spent warm in transit. A pallet that waits in a hot port, then a hot truck, can age more than the same hops would in months of cold storage. Pay for cold shipping on aroma varieties if you can, particularly for beers where hop aroma is the main flavour. Put a small temperature logger inside a carton to see what your route does. The same method applies to your finished beer, as discussed in our guide to the hot-country cold chain.

Store hops cold and away from oxygen. A freezer at -10 °C or colder is ideal for pellets. A fridge is much better than room temperature. Suppliers commonly advise cold storage, with freezing for long periods. Keep packs sealed and upright. When you open a pack, use what you need, squeeze out the air, reseal with a heat sealer or a vacuum sealer and return it to the cold quickly.

Avoid moisture. Condensation forms when cold packs are opened in a warm, humid room. Let the sealed pack warm slightly before cutting, or open it in the coolest part of the room and work fast.

Do not buy more hops than you can use while they are fresh. Estimate how many kilograms each recipe uses per month, add a safety margin for late deliveries and buy to that. Holding a year of stock for aroma varieties is a bet that cold storage works perfectly. Keep a log of purchase date, lot and HSI. Use older lots first, in bittering additions where aroma matters less.

Bittering is a good place to save. Alpha acid content differs from lot to lot and falls in storage, so adjust additions when the lot changes. For example, a hop that tested at 12 per cent alpha acids when bought may give less bitterness a year later. Test or recalculate rather than assuming.
Alternatives when fresh hops are hard to get

Hop extracts and isomerised products give bitterness that is stable at room temperature and are widely used by large breweries. They do not carry the aroma. Hop oils and some processed products exist for aroma, but their flavour differs from whole hops. Late additions, whirlpool and dry hop timing also change how much aroma survives in the beer. If your supply chain is long, build the recipe around hops that hold up and put the delicate aroma hops in beers you can serve fresh.

Have a look at the malt side of the same supply problem in importing malt for a small brewery. If you work on a homebrew scale and live far from a supplier, buying ingredients with no shop nearby covers a version of the same issue.
faqs: How should I store hop pellets?
Cold, sealed and away from oxygen. A freezer at -10 °C or colder is best for long storage. Reseal opened packs tightly.
What is the hop storage index?
It is a lab measure of how much a hop sample has aged. A lower figure means fresher hops. Ask your supplier whether they test it.
Do pellets last longer than whole cones?
Generally yes. Pellets are denser and easier to pack with little air, so they age more slowly under the same conditions.
Is cold shipping worth the cost?
For aroma hops in hop-forward beers, usually yes. For bittering hops used in a lager, ambient shipping may be acceptable.
